<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:prejudice}
  Introducing parabolic objects on a common ground with elliptic
  and hyperbolic ones we should warn against some common prejudices
  suggested by picture~\eqref{eq:eph-class}:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \label{it:par-is-zero} The parabolic case is unimportant (has
    ``zero measure'') in comparison to the elliptic and hyperbolic ones.
    As we shall see (e.g. Remark~\ref{re:par-more-cayley}
    and~\ref{re:focal-lenght}.\ref{it:more-lengths}) some geometrical features are richer in
    parabolic case.
  \item 
    \label{it:par-is-limit} The parabolic case is a limiting situation
    (a contraction) or an intermediate position between the elliptic
    and hyperbolic ones: all properties of the former can be guessed
    or obtained as a limit or an average from the latter two.
    Particularly this point of view is implicitly supposed
    in~\cite{LavrentShabat77}.
    
    Although there are few confirmations of this (e.g.
    Fig.~\ref{fig:unit-disks}(\(E\))--(\(H\))), we shall see (e.g.
    Remark~\ref{re:par-is-not-limit}) that some properties of the
    parabolic case cannot be straightforwardly guessed from a
    combination of the elliptic and hyperbolic cases.
  \item All three EPH cases are even less disjoint than it is usually
    thought. For example, there are meaningful notions of \emph{centre of
      a parabola}~\eqref{de:center-first} or \emph{focus of
      a circle}~\eqref{eq:def-focus}.
  \item A (co-)invariant geometry is believed to be ``coordinate free''
    which sometimes is pushed to an absolute mantra. However our
    study within the Erlangen program framework reveals two useful notions
    (Defn.~\ref{de:center-first} and ~\eqref{eq:def-focus}) mentioned
    above which are defined by coordinate expressions and look very
    ``non-invariant'' on the first glance. 
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{re:klein-descartes}
  We should say a word or two on proofs in this paper.  Majority of
  them are done through symbolic computations performed in the
  paper~\cite{Kisil05b} on the base of \textsf{GiNaC}~\cite{GiNaC} computer
  algebra system. As a result we can reduce many proofs just to a
  one-line reference to the paper~\cite{Kisil05b}. In a sense this is
  the complete fulfilment of the \emph{Cartesian program} of reducing
  geometry to algebra with the latter to be done by straightforward
  \emph{mechanical calculations}.  Therefore the Erlangen program is
  nicely compatible with the Cartesian approach: the former defines
  the set of geometrical object with invariant properties and the
  latter provides a toolbox for their study. Another example of their
  unification in the field of non-commutative geometry was discussed
  in~\cite{Kisil02c}.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- problem-1: body_md -->
\label{prob:higher-dim-gener}
  To which extend the subject presented here can be generalised to
  higher dimensions?
<!-- end problem-1 -->
<!-- conv-1: body_md -->
\label{co:eph-and-a}
  There will be three different Clifford algebras \({\ensuremath{ 
\mathcal{C}\kern-0.12em\ell(e)}}\),
  \({\ensuremath{ 
\mathcal{C}\kern-0.12em\ell(p)}}\), \({\ensuremath{ 
\mathcal{C}\kern-0.12em\ell(h)}}\) corresponding to \emph{elliptic},
  \emph{parabolic}, and \emph{hyperbolic} cases respectively. The
  notation \({\ensuremath{ 
\mathcal{C}\kern-0.12em\ell(\sigma)}}\), with assumed values \(\sigma=-1\),
  \(0\), \(1\), refers to \emph{any} of these three algebras.
<!-- end conv-1 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{re:dual-double}
  A part of this paper can be rewritten in terms of complex, dual
  and double numbers and it will have some common points with
  Supplement~C of the book~\cite{Yaglom79}. However the usage of
  Clifford algebras provides some facilities which do not have natural
  equivalent in complex numbers, see Rem.~\ref{re:dual-limit}. Moreover
  the language of Clifford algebras is more uniform and also allows
  straightforward generalisations to higher
  dimensions~\cite{Kisil96d}.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{le:an-action}
For any type of the Clifford algebra \({\ensuremath{ 
\mathcal{C}\kern-0.12em\ell(\sigma)}}\):
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item The subgroup \(N\) defines shifts \(ue_0+ve_1 \mapsto
    (u+\nu)e_0+ve_1 \) along the ``real'' axis \(U\) by
    \(\nu\).\\
    The vector field of the derived representation is \(dN_a{(u,v)}=(1,0)\).
  \item The subgroup \(A\) defines dilations \(ue_0+ve_1 \mapsto
    \alpha^{-2}(ue_0+ve_1)\) by the factor \(\alpha^{-2}\) which fixes origin
    \((0,0)\).\\
    The vector field of the derived representation is \(dA_a{(u,v)}=(2u,2v)\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{le:k-orbit-gen}
  A \(K\)-orbit in \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{\sigma}_{}{}}\) passing the point
  \((0,t)\) has the following equation: 
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:k-orbit-eq}
    (u^2-\sigma v^2)-2v\frac{t^{-1}-\sigma t }{2}+1=0, \qquad
    \text{where } \sigma = e_1^2 \ (\textrm{i.e } -1, 0 \textrm{ or } 1).
  \end{equation}
  The curvature of a \(K\)-orbit at point \((0,t)\) is equal to 
  \begin{displaymath}
    \kappa=\frac{2t}{1+\sigma t^2}.
  \end{displaymath}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{le:k-action}
  \begin{enumerate}
    \renewcommand{(\ifcase\csname c@enumi\endcsname a\or e\or p\or h\fi)}{(\ifcase\csname c@enumi\endcsname a\or e\or p\or h\fi)}
  \item \label{item:circle-desc} 
    For \({\ensuremath{ 
\mathcal{C}\kern-0.12em\ell(e)}}\) the orbits of \(K\) are circles, they are
    coaxal~\cite{CoxeterGreitzer}*{\S~2.3} with the real line being
    the radical axis. A circle with centre
     at \((0, (v+v^{-1})/2)\) passing through two points \((0,v)\)
    and \((0,v^{-1})\).\\
    The vector field of the derived representation is
    \(dK_e{(u,v)}=(u^2-v^2+1, 2uv)\). 
  \item \label{item:parab-desc}
    For \({\ensuremath{ 
\mathcal{C}\kern-0.12em\ell(p)}}\) the orbits of \(K\) are parabolas with the
    vertical axis \(V\). A parabola passing through \((0,v/2)\) has horizontal
    directrix passing through \((0, v-v^{-1}/2)\) 
    and focus at \((0,(v+v^{-1})/2)\). \\
    The vector field of the derived representation is
    \(dK_p{(u,v)}=(u^2+1, 2uv)\).
  \item \label{item:hyperb-desc}
    For \({\ensuremath{ 
\mathcal{C}\kern-0.12em\ell(h)}}\) the orbits of \(K\) are hyperbolas with
    asymptotes parallel to lines \(u=\pm v\). A hyperbola passing
    through the point \((0,v)\) has the focal distance
    \(2p\), where \(p=\frac{v^2+1}{\sqrt{2}v}\) and the upper focus
    is located at \((0,f)\) with:
    \begin{displaymath}
    f=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
      p-\sqrt{\frac{p^2}{2}-1}, &\textrm{ for } 0<v<1; \textrm{
        and }\\
      p+\sqrt{\frac{p^2}{2}-1}, & \textrm{ for } v\geq 1.
    \end{array}\right.
  \end{displaymath}
  The vector field of the derived representation is
    \(dK_h{(u,v)}=(u^2+v^2+1, 2uv)\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\(K\)-orbits may be obtained cases as follows: 
  \begin{enumerate}
    \renewcommand{(\ifcase\csname c@enumi\endcsname a\or e\or p\or h\fi)}{(\ifcase\csname c@enumi\endcsname a\or e\or p\or h\fi)}
  \item elliptic \(K\)-orbits are sections of cones~\eqref{eq:cones-fam} by the plane
    \(z=0\) (\(EE'\) on Fig.~\ref{fig:k-orbit-sect}); 
  \item parabolic \(K\)-orbits are sections of~\eqref{eq:cones-fam} by the plane
    \(y=\pm z\) (\(PP'\) on Fig.~\ref{fig:k-orbit-sect});
  \item hyperbolic   \(K\)-orbits are sections of~\eqref{eq:cones-fam} by the plane \(y=0\) 
    (\(HH'\) on Fig.~\ref{fig:k-orbit-sect});
  \end{enumerate}

  Moreover, each straight line generating a cone from the
  family~\eqref{eq:cones-fam} is crossing corresponding elliptic,
  parabolic and hyperbolic \(K\)-orbits at points with the same value of
  parameter \(\phi\)~\eqref{eq:iwasawa-param} of the subgroup \(K\).
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:orbits2}
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item The values of all three vector fields \(dK_e\), \(dK_p\) and \(dK_h\)
    coincide on the ``real'' \(U\)-axis \(v=0\), i.e. they are three
    different extensions into the domain of the same boundary
    condition. Another source of this: the axis \(U\) is the
    intersection of planes \(EE'\), \(PP'\) and \(HH'\) on
    Fig.~\ref{fig:k-orbit-sect}. 
  \item \label{it:hyp-orbit} The hyperbola passing through the point
    \((0,1)\) has the shortest focal length \(\sqrt{2}\) among all
    other hyperbolic orbits since it is the section of the cone
    \(x^2+(y-1)^2+z^2=0\) closest from the family to the plane
    \(HH'\).   
  \item Two hyperbolas passing through \((0,v)\) and \((0,v^{-1})\)
    have the same focal length since they are sections of two cones
    with the same distance from \(HH'\). Moreover, two such hyperbolas
    in the lower- and upper half-planes passing the points
    \((0,v)\) and \((0,-v^{-1})\) are sections of the same
    double-sided cone.  They are related to each other as explained in
    Remark~\ref{rem:two-cver}.\ref{it:hyp-object}.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{le:fix-subgroups}
  The fix group of the point \(e_1\) is
  \begin{enumerate}
    \renewcommand{(\ifcase\csname c@enumi\endcsname a\or e\or p\or h\fi)}{(\ifcase\csname c@enumi\endcsname a\or e\or p\or h\fi)}
  \item\label{it:fix-group-ell} 
    the subgroup \(K'_e=K\) in the elliptic case. Thus the
    elliptic upper half-plane is a model for the homogeneous space
    \(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}/K\); 
  \item \label{it:fix-group-par}
    the subgroup \(N'_p\) of matrices
    \begin{equation}
      \label{eq:par-fix-subgroup}
      \begin{pmatrix}
        1&0\\
         \nu e_0 & 1
      \end{pmatrix}
      =
      \begin{pmatrix}
        0&e_0\\
        e_0 & 0
      \end{pmatrix}
      \begin{pmatrix}
        1&\nu e_0\\
         0& 1
      \end{pmatrix}
      \begin{pmatrix}
        0&-e_0\\
        -e_0 & 0
      \end{pmatrix}
    \end{equation}
    in the parabolic case.  It also fixes any point \(ve1\).  It is
    conjugate to subgroup \(N\), thus the parabolic upper half-plane is
    a model for the homogeneous space \(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}/N\);
  \item \label{it:fix-group-hyp}
    the subgroup \(A'_h\) of matrices
    \begin{equation}
      \label{eq:hyp-fix-subgroup}
      \begin{pmatrix}
        \cosh(\tau) & \sinh(\tau)e_0\\
        -\sinh(\tau)e_0 & \cosh(\tau) 
      \end{pmatrix} =
      \frac{1}{2}
      \begin{pmatrix}
        1 & -e_0\\
        -e_0 & 1
      \end{pmatrix}
      \begin{pmatrix}
        e^\tau & 0\\
        0 & e^{-\tau}
      \end{pmatrix}
      \begin{pmatrix}
        1 & e_0\\
        e_0 & 1
      \end{pmatrix},
    \end{equation}
    in the hyperbolic case. It is conjugate to subgroup \(A\), thus
    two copies of the upper halfplane (see
    Section~\ref{sec:invar-upper-half}) is a model for \(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}/A\).
  \end{enumerate}

  Moreover, vectors fields of these actions are \((u^2+\sigma(v^2-1), 2uv)\) for
  the corresponding values of \(\sigma\).
  Orbits of the fix groups satisfy to the equation:
  \begin{displaymath}
        (u^2-\sigma v^2)-2lv-\sigma=0, \qquad
    \text{where } l\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}}.
  \end{displaymath}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
  \item   Note that we can uniformly express the fix-subgroups of \(e_1\) in
    all EPH cases by
    matrices of the form:
    \begin{displaymath}
      \begin{pmatrix}
        a & -\sigma e_0b\\
        -e_0b & a
      \end{pmatrix},\qquad \text{ where } a^2-\sigma b^2=1.
    \end{displaymath}
  \item In the hyperbolic case the subgroup \(A'_h\) may be extended to a
    subgroup \(A''_h\) by the element \(
    \begin{pmatrix}
      0&e_0\\e_0&0
    \end{pmatrix}\), which flips upper and lower half-planes (see
    Section~\ref{sec:invar-upper-half}).  The subgroup \(A''_h\) fixes
    the set \(\{e_1,-e_1\}\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{le:fix-ax+b-gen-sl2}
  M\"obius action of \(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\) in each EPH case is generated by
  action  the corresponding fix-subgroup (\(A''_h\) in the hyperbolic case) and
  actions of the \(ax+b\) group, e.g. subgroups \(A\) and \(N\).
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
The \(ax+b\) group transitively acts on the upper or lower half-plane. Thus
  for any \(g\in\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\) there is \(h\) in \(ax+b\) group such that
  \(h^{-1}g\) either fixes \(e_1\) or sends it to \(-e_1\). Thus
  \(h^{-1}g\) is in the corresponding fix-group.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
We use the word \emph{cycle} to denote loci in \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{\sigma}_{}{}}\)
  defined by the equation:
\begin{subequations}
  \label{eq:cycle-def}
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:cycle-def-cliff}
    -k(u e_0+v e_1)^2-2\left\langle (l,n),(u,v) 
        \right\rangle\ifx\relax\relax\else_{\relax}\fi+m=0
  \end{equation}
  or equivalently (avoiding any reference to Clifford algebra generators): 
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:cycle-def-real}
    k(u^2-\sigma v^2)-2lu-2nv+m=0, \qquad \text{ where } \sigma = e_1^2,
  \end{equation}
  or equivalently (using \emph{only} Clifford algebra operations,
  cf.~\cite{Yaglom79}*{Supl.~C(42a)}):  
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:cycle-def-compl}
    K w^2+Lw-wL+M=0,
  \end{equation}
  where \(w= ue_0+ve_1\), \(K=-ke_{01}\), \(L=-n e_0+l e_1\),
  \(M=me_{01}\).
\end{subequations}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{de:center-first}
  \emph{\(\mathring{\sigma}\)-Centre} of the \(\sigma\)-cycle~\eqref{eq:cycle-def}
  for any EPH case is the point \(\left(\frac{l}{k},
    -\mathring{\sigma}\frac{n}{k}\right)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{\sigma}_{}{}}\). Notions of e-centre,
  p-centre, h-centre are used along the adopted EPH notations.
  
  Centres of straight lines are at infinity, see  subsection~\ref{sec:comp-spra}.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{re:different-signatures}
  Here we use a signature \(\mathring{\sigma}=-1\), \(0\) or \(1\) of a  Clifford
  algebra which is not related to the signature \(\sigma\) of the
  space \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{\sigma}_{}{}}\). We will need also a third signature
  \(\breve{\sigma}\) to describe the geometry of cycles in
  Defn.~\ref{de:cycle-2-matrix}.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{le:invariance-of-cycles}
  M\"obius transformations preserve the cycles in the
  upper   half-plane, i.e.:
  \begin{enumerate}
    \renewcommand{(\ifcase\csname c@enumi\endcsname a\or e\or p\or h\fi)}{(\ifcase\csname c@enumi\endcsname a\or e\or p\or h\fi)}
  \item For \({\ensuremath{ 
\mathcal{C}\kern-0.12em\ell(e)}}\) M\"obius transformations map circles to circles.
  \item For \({\ensuremath{ 
\mathcal{C}\kern-0.12em\ell(p)}}\) M\"obius transformations map parabolas to parabolas.
  \item For \({\ensuremath{ 
\mathcal{C}\kern-0.12em\ell(h)}}\) M\"obius transformations map hyperbolas to hyperbolas. 
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
\begin{figure}[htbp]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[scale=1.1]{cycle-inv.eps}
  \caption[The decomposition of an arbitrary M\"obius
  transformation]{Decomposition of an arbitrary M\"obius
    transformation \(g\) into a product \(g=g_a g_n g_k g_a' g_n'\).}
  \label{fig:moeb-decomp}
\end{figure}
  Our first observation is that the subgroups \(A\) and \(N\) obviously
  preserve all circles, parabolas, hyperbolas and straight lines in all
  \({\ensuremath{ 
\mathcal{C}\kern-0.12em\ell(\sigma)}}\). Thus we use subgroups \(A\) and \(N\) to  fit a given
  cycle exactly on a particular orbit of subgroup \(K\) shown on
  Fig.~\ref{fig:k-subgroup} of the corresponding type. 

  To this end for an arbitrary cycle \(S\) we can find \(g_n'\in N\)
  which puts centre of \(S\) on the \(V\)-axis, see
  Fig.~\ref{fig:moeb-decomp}. Then there is a unique \(g_a'\in A\)
  which scales it exactly to an orbit of \(K\), e.g. for a
  circle passing through points \((0,v_1)\) and \((0,v_2)\) the scaling
  factor is \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{v_1v_2}}\) according to
  Lemma~\ref{le:k-action}.\ref{item:circle-desc}. Let \(g'=g_a' g_n'\), then for any
  element \(g\in \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\) using the Iwasawa decomposition of \(g
  g'^{-1}=g_a g_n g_k\) we get the presentation \(g=g_a g_n g_k g_a'
  g_n'\) with \(g_a, g_a'\in A\), \(g_n, g_n'\in N\) and \(g_k \in
  K\).

  Then the image \(g'S\) of the cycle \(S\) under \(g'=g_a' g_n'\)
  is a cycle itself in the obvious way, then \(g_k (g'S)\) is again a
  cycle since \(g'S\) was arranged to coincide with a \(K\)-orbit, and
  finally  \(gS=g_a g_n (g_k (g'S))\) is a cycle due to the obvious
  action of \(g_a g_n\), see Fig.~\ref{fig:moeb-decomp} for an
  illustration.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{de:cycle-2-matrix}  
  Let \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}^{3}_{}{}}\) be the projective space, i.e. collection of
  the rays passing through points in \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{4}_{}{}}\). We define the
  following two identifications (depending from some additional
  parameters \(\sigma\), \(\breve{\sigma}\) and \(s\) described below) which map a
  point \((k, l, n, m)\in \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}^{3}_{}{}}\) to:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item[\(Q\):]                           
    the cycle (quadric) \({ C^{}_{}}\) on
    \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{\sigma}_{}{}}\)
    defined by the equations~\eqref{eq:cycle-def} with constant
    parameters \(k\), \(l\), \(n\), \(m\):
    \begin{equation}
      \label{eq:cycle-def-1}
          -k(e_0u+e_1v)^2-2\left\langle (l,n),(u,v) 
        \right\rangle\ifx\relax\relax\else_{\relax}\fi+m=0,
    \end{equation}
     for some \({\ensuremath{ 
\mathcal{C}\kern-0.12em\ell(\sigma)}}\) with generators \(e_0^2=-1\), \(e_1^2=\sigma\).
  \item[\(M\):]                         
    the ray of \(2\times 2\) matrices 
    passing through 
    \begin{equation}
      \label{eq:matrix-for-cycle}
      { C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} = \begin{pmatrix}
      l\breve{e}_0+sn\breve{e}_1 & m\\
      k & -l\breve{e}_0-sn\breve{e}_1
    \end{pmatrix} \in M_2({\ensuremath{ 
\mathcal{C}\kern-0.12em\ell(\breve{\sigma})}}), \text{ with }
     \breve{e}_0^2=-1, \breve{e}_1^2=\breve{\sigma},
    \end{equation}
    i.e. generators \(\breve{e}_0\) and \(\breve{e}_1\) of \({\ensuremath{ 
\mathcal{C}\kern-0.12em\ell(\breve{\sigma})}}\)
    can be \emph{of any type}: elliptic, parabolic or hyperbolic
    regardless of the \({\ensuremath{ 
\mathcal{C}\kern-0.12em\ell(\sigma)}}\) in~\eqref{eq:cycle-def-1}.
                                           
                                                                      
                                                                         
  \end{itemize}
   The meaningful values of parameters \(\sigma\), \(\breve{\sigma}\) and \(s\)
   are \(-1\), \(0\) or \(1\), and in many cases \(s\) is equal to
   \(\sigma\).
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
A hint for the composition of the matrix~\eqref{eq:matrix-for-cycle}
  is provided by the following identity:
  \begin{displaymath}
    \begin{pmatrix} 
      1&w
    \end{pmatrix}
    \begin{pmatrix} 
      L&M\\K&-L
    \end{pmatrix}
    \begin{pmatrix} 
      w\\1
    \end{pmatrix}=     w K w+Lw-wL+M,
  \end{displaymath}
  which realises the equation~\eqref{eq:cycle-def-compl} of a cycle.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{pr:transform-cycles} 
  A cycle \(-k(e_0u+e_1v)^2-2\left\langle (l,n),(u,v) 
        \right\rangle\ifx\relax\relax\else_{\relax}\fi+m=0\) is
  transformed by \(g\in\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\) into the cycle
  \(-\tilde{k}(e_0u+e_1v)^2-2\left\langle (\tilde{l},
    \tilde{n}),(u,v) 
        \right\rangle\ifx\relax\relax\else_{\relax}\fi+\tilde{m}=0\) such that
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:cycle-transform-short}
    {\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}=  g{ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}g^{-1}
  \end{equation}
  for any Clifford algebras \({\ensuremath{ 
\mathcal{C}\kern-0.12em\ell(\sigma)}}\) and
  \({\ensuremath{ 
\mathcal{C}\kern-0.12em\ell(\breve{\sigma})}}\). Explicitly this means:
  \begin{eqnarray}
    \label{eq:cycle-transform}
    \lefteqn{
    \begin{pmatrix}
      \tilde{l}\breve{e}_0+s\tilde{n}\breve{e}_1 & \tilde{m}\\
      \tilde{k} & -\tilde{l}\breve{e}_0-s\tilde{n}\breve{e}_1
    \end{pmatrix}
  }\qquad\qquad \\
    &=&
    \begin{pmatrix}
      a & b\breve{e}_0\\
      -c\breve{e}_0 & d
    \end{pmatrix}
    \begin{pmatrix}
      l\breve{e}_0+sn\breve{e}_1 & m\\
      k & -l\breve{e}_0-sn\breve{e}_1
    \end{pmatrix}
    \begin{pmatrix}
      d & -b\breve{e}_0\\
      c\breve{e}_0 & a
    \end{pmatrix}. \nonumber 
  \end{eqnarray}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
It is already established in the elliptic and hyperbolic cases for
  \(\sigma=\breve{\sigma}\), see \cite{Cnops02a}. For all EPH cases (including
  parabolic) it can be done by the direct calculation in
  \textsf{GiNaC}~\cite{Kisil05b}*{\S~\ref{G-sec:mobi-invar-cycl}}. An
  alternative idea of an elegant proof based on the zero-radius cycles
  and orthogonality (see below) may be borrowed from~\cite{Cnops02a}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:orbits}
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item   
    \label{it:real-line-inv}
    The real axis \(v=0\) is represented by the ray coming through
  \((0,0,1,0)\) and a matrix \(
  \begin{pmatrix}
    s\breve{e}_1&0\\
    0&-s\breve{e}_1
  \end{pmatrix}\). For any \(
  \begin{pmatrix}
    a&b\breve{e}_0\\
    -c\breve{e}_0& d
  \end{pmatrix}\in \ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\) we have:
  \begin{displaymath}
    \begin{pmatrix}
      a&b\breve{e}_0\\
      -c\breve{e}_0& d
    \end{pmatrix}
    \begin{pmatrix}
      s\breve{e}_1&0\\
      0&-s\breve{e}_1
    \end{pmatrix}
    \begin{pmatrix}
      d & -b\breve{e}_0\\
      c\breve{e}_0 & a
    \end{pmatrix} =
    \begin{pmatrix}
      s\breve{e}_1&0\\
      0&-s\breve{e}_1
    \end{pmatrix},
  \end{displaymath}
  i.e. the real line is \(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\)-invariant.
\item 
  \label{it:k-orbit-similarity}
  A direct calculation in
  GiNaC~\cite{Kisil05b}*{\S~\ref{G-sec:transf-k-orbits}} shows that
  matrices representing cycles from~\eqref{eq:k-orbit-eq} are
  invariant under the similarity with elements of \(K\), thus they are
  indeed \(K\)-orbits.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{re:real-line-inv-0}
  Such a variety of choices is a consequence of the usage of \(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\)---a
  smaller group of symmetries in comparison to the all M\"obius maps
  of \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{2}_{}{}}\). The \(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\) group fixes the real line and consequently a
  decomposition of vectors into ``real'' (\(e_0\)) and ``imaginary''
  (\(e_1\)) parts is obvious. This permits to assign an arbitrary
  value to the square of the ``imaginary unit'' \(e_1e_0\).

  Geometric invariants defined below, e.g. orthogonalities in
  sections~\ref{sec:orthogonality} and~\ref{sec:focal-orthogonality},
  demonstrate ``awareness'' of the real line invariance in one way or
  another. We will call this the \emph{boundary effect} in the
  upper half-plane geometry. The famous question
  on
    hearing drum's shape has a sister:
  \begin{quote}
  \emph{Can we see/feel the boundary from inside a domain?}
  \end{quote}
  Rems.~\ref{re:real-line-inv-1},~\ref{re:real-line-inv-2}
  and~\ref{re:real-line-inv-3} provide hints for positive answers.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
Any implementation of cycles shown on~\eqref{eq:cycles-diagram} by
  the dotted arrow for any combination of \(\sigma\),
  \(\breve{\sigma}\) and \(s\) intertwines two actions of \(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\): by
  matrix conjugation~\eqref{eq:cycle-transform-short} and M\"obius
  transformations~\eqref{eq:moebius-def}.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
A similar representation of circles by \(2\times 2\) complex
  matrices which intertwines M\"obius transformations and matrix
  conjugations was used recently by A.A.~Kirillov~\cite{Kirillov06} in
  the study of the Apollonian gasket. Kirillov's matrix
  realisation~\cite{Kirillov06} of a cycle has an attractive
  ``self-adjoint'' form:
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:kirrilov-matrix}
    { C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} = \begin{pmatrix}
      m & l\breve{e}_0+sn\breve{e}_1 \\
      -l\breve{e}_0-sn\breve{e}_1 & k  
    \end{pmatrix} \text{ (in notations of this paper)}.
  \end{equation}
  Note that the matrix inverse to~\eqref{eq:kirrilov-matrix}  is intertwined with the SFSCc
  presentation~\eqref{eq:matrix-for-cycle} by the matrix \(
  \begin{pmatrix}
    0&1\\1&0
  \end{pmatrix}\).
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{de:inner-product}
  \emph{Inner \(\breve{\sigma}\)-product} of two cycles is given by the trace of their
  product as matrices:
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:inner-product}
    \left\langle { C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}},{\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} 
        \right\rangle\ifx\relax\relax\else_{\relax}\fi = \mathop{tr}({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}{\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}).
  \end{equation}
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{de:normalisation}
  A SFSCc matrix representing a cycle is said to be \(k\)-normalised if its
  \((2,1)\)-element  is \(1\) and it is \(\det\)-normalised if its
  determinant is equal \(1\).
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{de:focus}
  \emph{\(\mathring{\sigma}\)-Focus} of a cycle \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\)
  is the point in \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{\sigma}_{}{}}\)
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:def-focus}
    f_{\mathring{\sigma}}=\left(\frac{l}{k}, -\frac{\det{ C^{s}_{\mathring{\sigma}}}}{2nk}\right)
    \quad \text{ or  explicitly } \quad
    f_{\mathring{\sigma}} =\left(\frac{l}{k}, \frac{mk-l^2+\mathring{\sigma} n^2}{2nk}\right).
  \end{equation}
  We also use \emph{e-focus}, \emph{p-focus}, \emph{h-focus} and
  \emph{\(\mathring{\sigma}\)-focus}, in line with
  Convention~\ref{co:eph-and-a} to take into account of the type of
  \({\ensuremath{ 
\mathcal{C}\kern-0.12em\ell(\mathring{\sigma})}}\).

  \emph{Focal length} of a cycle is \(\frac{n}{2k}\).
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
Note that focus of \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) is independent of the sign of
  \(s\). Geometrical meaning of focus is as follows. 
  If a cycle is realised in the parabolic space \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{p}_{}{}}\)
  \emph{h-focus}, \emph{p-focus}, \emph{e-focus} are correspondingly
  geometrical focus of the parabola, its vertex and the point on
  directrix nearest to the vertex, see
  Fig.~\ref{fig:eph-cycle}(b). Thus the traditional focus is h-focus
  in our notations.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{de:zero-radius-cycle}
  \emph{\(\breve{\sigma}\)-Zero-radius cycles} are defined by the condition
  \(\det({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}})=0\), i.e. are explicitly given by matrices
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:zero-cycle-matrix}
    \begin{pmatrix}
      y & -y^2\\
      1 & -y
    \end{pmatrix} =\frac{1}{2}
    \begin{pmatrix}
      y & y\\
      1 & 1
    \end{pmatrix}
    \begin{pmatrix}
      1 & -y\\
      1 & -y
    \end{pmatrix} = 
    \begin{pmatrix}
      \breve{e}_0 u+\breve{e}_1 v & u^2-\breve{\sigma} v^2\\
      1 & -\breve{e}_0 u-\breve{e}_1 v
    \end{pmatrix}, 
  \end{equation}
  where  \(y=\breve{e}_0 u+\breve{e}_1 v\).
  We denote such a \(\breve{\sigma}\)-zero-radius cycle by \( Z^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}(y)\).
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\label{re:real-line-inv-1}
  The above ``touching'' property of zero-radius cycles for \(\breve{\sigma}=0\)
  is an example of boundary effect inside the domain mentioned in
  Rem.~\ref{re:real-line-inv-0}. It is not surprising after all since
  \(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\) action on the upper half-plane may be considered as an
  extension of its action on the real axis.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{le:moeb-conj-z-cycle}
  The conjugate \(g^{-1} Z^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}(y)g\) of a \(\breve{\sigma}\)-zero-radius cycle
  \( Z^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}(y)\) with \(g\in\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\) is a \(\breve{\sigma}\)-zero-radius cycle
  \( Z^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}(g\cdot y)\) with centre at \(g\cdot y\)---the M\"obius
  transform of the centre of \( Z^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}(y)\).
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
This may be calculated in \textsf{GiNaC}~\cite{Kisil05b}*{\S~\ref{G-sec:mobi-invar-cycl}}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{de:self-adj-cycle}
   \emph{Self-adjoint cycle} for \(\breve{\sigma}\neq 0\) are defined by the
   condition \(\Re \left\langle { C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}, R^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}} 
        \right\rangle\ifx\relax\relax\else_{\relax}\fi=0\),
   where \( R^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}\) corresponds to the ``real'' axis
   \(v=0\) and \(\Re\) denotes the real part of a Clifford number.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{le:invariant-cycles}
  Self-adjoint cycles form a family, which is invariant under the M\"obius
  transformations.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
The proof is either geometrically obvious from the transformations
  described in Section~\ref{sec:mobi-transf}, or follows analytically
  from the action described in Proposition~\ref{pr:transform-cycles}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
Geometric objects, which are invariant under infinitesimal action of \(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\), were
  studied recently in papers~\cites{KonovenkoLychagin08a,Konovenko09a}.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
\label{de:orthogonality-first}
  Two cycles \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) and \({\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) are
  \emph{\(\breve{\sigma}\)-orthogonal} if the real part of their inner
  product~\eqref{eq:inner-product} vanishes:
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:orthogonality-first}
    \Re\left\langle { C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}},{\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} 
        \right\rangle\ifx\relax\relax\else_{\relax}\fi
    = 0\quad \text{ or, equivalently, }\quad
    \left\langle { C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}},{\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} 
        \right\rangle\ifx\relax\relax\else_{\relax}\fi+\left\langle {\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}},{ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} 
        \right\rangle\ifx\relax\relax\else_{\relax}\fi
    = 0
  \end{equation}
  In light of~\eqref{eq:trace-det} the zero-radius
  cycles (Defn.~\ref{de:zero-radius-cycle}) are also called
  \emph{self-orthogonal} or \emph{isotropic}.
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
The \(\breve{\sigma}\)-orthogonality condition~\eqref{eq:orthogonality-first} is invariant
  under M\"obius transformations.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
It immediately follows from Definition~\ref{de:orthogonality-first},
  formula~\eqref{eq:cycle-transform-short} and the invariance of trace under
  similarity.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{le:first-orthogonality}
    The
    \(\breve{\sigma}\)-orthogonality~\eqref{eq:orthogonality-first} of
    cycles \({\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) and
    \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) is given through their defining
    equation~\eqref{eq:cycle-def-1} coefficients by
    \begin{eqnarray}
      \label{eq:first-ortho-gen}
      2\breve{\sigma}\tilde{n}n-2\tilde{l}l+\tilde{k}m+\tilde{m}k = 0.
    \end{eqnarray}
    or specifically by
    \begin{eqnarray}
      \label{eq:first-ortho-e}
      -2\tilde{n}n-2\tilde{l}l+\tilde{k}m+\tilde{m}k &=& 0,\\
      \label{eq:first-ortho-p}
      -2\tilde{l}l+\tilde{k}m+\tilde{m}k &=& 0,\\
      \label{eq:first-ortho-h}
      2\tilde{n}n-2\tilde{l}l+\tilde{k}m+\tilde{m}k &=& 0
    \end{eqnarray}
    in the elliptic, parabolic and hyperbolic cases of \({\ensuremath{ 
\mathcal{C}\kern-0.12em\ell(\sigma)}}\) correspondingly.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
  \item A \(\breve{\sigma}\)-self-orthogonal cycle is
    \(\breve{\sigma}\)-zero-radius one~\eqref{eq:zero-cycle-matrix}.
  \item For \(\breve{\sigma}=\pm 1\) there is no non-trivial cycle
    orthogonal to all other non-trivial cycles.\\
    For \(\breve{\sigma}=0\) only the real axis \(v=0\) is orthogonal
    to all other non-trivial cycles.
  \item For \(\breve{\sigma}=\pm 1\) any cycle is uniquely defined
    by the family of cycles orthogonal to it,
    i.e. \(({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}^\perp)^\perp=\{{ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\}\) .\\ 
    For \(\breve{\sigma}= 0\) the set
    \(({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}^\perp)^\perp\) consists of all cycles
    which have the same roots as \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\),
    see middle column of pictures in Fig.~\ref{fig:orthogonality1}.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{le:zero-radius-otho}
  A cycle \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) is
  \(\breve{\sigma}\)-orthogonal to \(\sigma\)-zero-radius cycle
  \( Z^{s}_{\sigma }(u,v)\) if 
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:ortho-zero-rad}
    k(u^2 k- \sigma v^2) - 2\left\langle (l,n),(u, \breve{\sigma} v) 
        \right\rangle\ifx\relax\relax\else_{\relax}\fi+m =0,
  \end{equation}
  i.e. \(\sigma\)-implementation of \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) is
  passing through the point \((u, \breve{\sigma} v)\), which \(\breve{\sigma}\)-centre of
  \( Z^{s}_{\sigma}(u,v)\).
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{pr:cycle-map-ext}
  Let \(T: \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}^{3}_{}{}} \rightarrow \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}^{3}_{}{}}\) is
  an orthogonality preserving map of the cycles space,
  i.e. \(\left\langle { C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}},{\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} 
        \right\rangle\ifx\relax\relax\else_{\relax}\fi=0 \
    \Leftrightarrow  \left\langle T{ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}},T{\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} 
        \right\rangle\ifx\relax\relax\else_{\relax}\fi=0\). Then
    for \(\sigma\neq 0\) there is a map \(T_\sigma : \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{\sigma}_{}{}}
    \rightarrow\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{\sigma}_{}{}}\), such that \(Q\) intertwines \(T\) and
    \(T_\sigma \):
    \begin{equation}
      \label{eq:Q-intertwine}
       Q T_\sigma  = T Q. 
    \end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
If \(T\) preserves the orthogonality (i.e. the inner
  product~\eqref{eq:inner-product} and consequently the determinant
  from~\eqref{eq:trace-det}) then by the image
  \(T Z^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}(u,v)\) of a zero-radius cycle
  \( Z^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}(u,v)\) is again a zero-radius cycle
  \( Z^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}(u_1,v_1)\) and we can define \(T_\sigma \) by the identity
  \(T_\sigma : (u,v)\mapsto (u_1,v_1)\).  

  To prove the intertwining property~\eqref{eq:Q-intertwine} we need
  to show that if a cycle \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) passes through \((u,v)\)
  then  the image \(T{ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) passes through \(T_\sigma
  (u,v)\). However for \(\sigma\neq 0\) this is a consequence of the
  \(T\)-invariance of orthogonality and the expression of the
  point-to-cycle incidence through the orthogonality from
  Lemma~\ref{le:zero-radius-otho}.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
Let \(T_i: \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}^{3}_{}{}} \rightarrow \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}^{3}_{}{}}\), \(i=1,2\) are
  two orthogonality preserving maps of the cycles space. If they
  coincide on the subspace of \(\breve{\sigma}\)-zero-radius cycles, \(\breve{\sigma}\neq
  0\), then they are identical in the whole \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}^{3}_{}{}}\).
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
\label{re:local-ortho}
  Note, that the orthogonality is reduced to local notion in terms of
  tangent lines to cycles in their intersection points \emph{only for
    \(\sigma\breve{\sigma}=1\)}, i.e. this happens only in NW and SE
  corners of Fig.~\ref{fig:orthogonality1}.  In other cases the local
  condition can be formulated in term of ``ghost'' cycle defined below.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{pr:ghost-cycle}
  Let cycles \({ C^{}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) and \({\tilde C^{}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) be
  \(\breve{\sigma}\)-orthogonal. For their \(\sigma\)-implementations we define
  the \emph{ghost cycle} \({\hat C^{}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) by the following two
  conditions:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \label{item:centre-centre-rel}
    \(\chi(\sigma)\)-centre of \({\hat C^{}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) coincides
    with  \(\breve{\sigma}\)-centre of \({ C^{}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\).
  \item Determinant of  \({\hat C^{1}_{\sigma}}\) is equal to
    determinant of \({ C^{\chi(\breve{\sigma})}_{\sigma}}\).
  \end{enumerate}
  Then:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item   \({\hat C^{}_{\sigma}}\) coincides with
    \({ C^{}_{\sigma}}\) if \(\sigma \breve{\sigma}=1\);
  \item   \({\hat C^{}_{\sigma}}\) has common roots (real or imaginary)
    with \({ C^{}_{\sigma}}\);
  \item In the \(\sigma\)-implementation the tangent line to
    \({\tilde C^{}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) at points of its intersections with the
    ghost cycle \({\hat C^{}_{\sigma}}\) are passing the
    \(\sigma\)-centre of  \({\hat C^{}_{\sigma}}\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The calculations are done in \textsf{GiNaC}, see~\cite{Kisil05b}*{\S~\ref{G-sec:ghost-cycle}}.
  For illustration see Fig.~\ref{fig:orthogonality1}, where the ghost
  cycle is shown by the black dashed line.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
\label{re:real-line-inv-2}
  Elliptic and hyperbolic ghost cycles are symmetric in the real line,
  the parabolic ghost cycle has its centre on it, see
  Fig.~\ref{fig:orthogonality1}. This is an illustration to the
  boundary effect from Rem.~\ref{re:real-line-inv-0}.
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
Let \(\det { C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} \neq 0\), then: 
  \label{le:cycle-conj-is-moeb}
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item The conjugation~\eqref{eq:cycle-conjugation} preserves the
    orthogonality relation~\eqref{eq:orthogonality-first}. 
  \item The image \({ C^{s_2}_{\sigma}}\tilde Z^{s_1}_{\sigma}(u,
    v){ C^{s_2}_{\sigma}}\) of a \(\sigma\)-zero-radius cycle
    \(\tilde Z^{s_1}_{\sigma}\) under the
    conjugation~\eqref{eq:cycle-conjugation} is a
    \(\sigma\)-zero-radius cycle \(\tilde Z^{s_1}_{\sigma}(u',
    v')\), where \((u',v')\) is calculated by the linear-fractional
    transformation~\eqref{eq:cycle-frac-linear}
    \((u',v')={ C^{s_1s_2}_{\sigma}}(u,v)\) associated to the cycle
    \({ C^{s_1s_2}_{\sigma}}\).
  \item Both formulae~\eqref{eq:cycle-frac-linear}
    and~\eqref{eq:cycle-conjugation} define the same transformation of
    the point space. 
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The first part is obvious, the second is calculated in
  \textsf{GiNaC}~\cite{Kisil05b}*{\S~\ref{G-sec:cycles-conjugation}}.  The last
  part follows from the first two and Prop.~\ref{pr:cycle-map-ext}.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
\label{def:inversion}
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item\label{item:inversion-orthogonality} \emph{Inversion} in a
    cycle \({ C^{s}_{\sigma}}\) sends a point \(p\) to the second point
    \(p'\) of intersection of all cycles orthogonal to
    \({ C^{s}_{\sigma}}\) and passing through \(p\).
  \item\label{item:inversion-reflection} \emph{Reflection} in a cycle
     \({ C^{s}_{\sigma}}\) is given by \(M^{-1}RM\) where \(M\) sends the
    cycle  \({ C^{s}_{\sigma}}\) into the horizontal axis and \(R\) is the mirror
    reflection in that axis.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- remark-15: body_md -->
\label{re:dual-limit} Here is a simple example where usage of
  complex (dual or double) numbers is weaker then Clifford algebras,
  see Rem.~\ref{re:dual-double}. A reflection of a cycle in the axis \(v=0\) is
  represented by the conjugation~\eqref{eq:cycle-conjugation} with
  the corresponding matrix \(
  \begin{pmatrix}
    \breve{e}_1&0\\0&-\breve{e}_1
  \end{pmatrix}\). The same transformation in term of complex numbers
  should involve a complex conjugation and thus cannot be expressed by
  multiplication.
<!-- end remark-15 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{pr:orthogonality-to-cycle}
  A cycle \({\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}                                       
                                                             
  \) is
  orthogonal to a cycle \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}              
                                                   
  \) if for any point \(u_1e_0+v_1e_1\in {\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\)
  the cycle \({\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) is also passing through its
  image
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:inversion-ortho}
    u_2e_0+v_2e_1                                 
    =\begin{pmatrix}
      le_0+sre_1 & m\\
      k & le_0+sre_1
    \end{pmatrix}
    (u_1e_0+v_1e_1)
  \end{equation}
  under the M\"obius transform defined by the matrix
  \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\). Thus the point
  \(u_2e_0+v_2e_1={ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}(u_1e_0+v_1e_1)\) is the inversion of
  \(u_1e_0+v_1e_1\) in \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\).
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The symbolic calculations done by \textsf{GiNaC}\cite{Kisil05b}*{\S~\ref{G-sec:orth-invers}}.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
The reflection~\ref{def:inversion}.\ref{item:inversion-reflection} of
  a zero-radius cycle \( Z^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}\) in a cycle \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) is
  given by the conjugation: \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} Z^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}{ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\).
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let \({\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) has the property \({\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}
  { C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} {\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} = \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}}\). Then
  \({\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}} {\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} =
  { C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\). Mirror reflection in the real line is given by the
  conjugation with \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}}\), thus the transformation described
  in~\ref{def:inversion}.\ref{item:inversion-reflection} is a conjugation with the cycle
  \({\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}} {\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} =
  { C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) and thus coincide with~\eqref{eq:inversion-ortho}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{le:cycle-refl-real-line}
  Let \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}=(k, l, n,m)\) be a cycle and for \(\breve{\sigma}\neq 0\)
  the \({\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) be given by \((k, l,
    n\pm\sqrt{\det{ C^{\sigma}_{\breve{\sigma}}}},m)\). Then 
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \({\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} { C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} {\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}
    = \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}}\) and \({\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}}
    {\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} =  { C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\)
  \item\label{it:inv-cycle-root}
    \({\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) and \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) have common
    roots.
  \item \label{it:inv-cycle-center}
    In the \(\breve{\sigma}\)-implementation the cycle \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) passes
    the centre of \({\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
This is calculated by
  \textsf{GiNaC}~\cite{Kisil05b}*{\S~\ref{G-sec:reflection-cycles}}. Also one
  can direct observe~\ref{le:cycle-refl-real-line}.\ref{it:inv-cycle-root} for real roots, since
  they are fixed points of the inversion. Also the transformation of
  \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) to a flat cycle implies that \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\)
  is passing the centre of inversion, hence~\ref{le:cycle-refl-real-line}.\ref{it:inv-cycle-center}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{pr:inv-2nd-kind-decomp}
  The inversion of second kind~\eqref{eq:invers-sec-kind} is a
  composition of three inversions:  in parabolas \(u^2- 2lu
  -4mv-m/k=0\), \(u^2- 2lu-m/k=0\), and the real line.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
See symbolic calculation in~\cite{Kisil05b}*{\S~\ref{G-sec:invers-second-kind}}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- remark-16: body_md -->
Yaglom in~\cite{Yaglom79}*{\S~10} considers the usual inversion (``of the
  first kind'') only in degenerated parabolas (``parabolic circles'')
  of the form \(u^2-2lu+m=0\). However the inversion of the second
  kind requires for its decomposition like in
  Prop.~\ref{pr:inv-2nd-kind-decomp} at least one inversion in a proper
  parabolic cycle \(u^2-2lu-2nv+m=0\). Thus such inversions are indeed
  of \emph{another kind} within Yaglom's framework~\cite{Yaglom79},
  but are not in our.

  Another important difference between inversions
  from~\cite{Yaglom79} and our wider set of 
  transformations~\eqref{eq:cycle-frac-linear} is what ``special''
  (vertical) lines does not form an invariant set, as can be
  seen from Fig.~\ref{fig:inversions}(c), and thus they are not
  ``special'' lines anymore.
<!-- end remark-16 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
\label{de:f-ortho}
  The \emph{focal orthogonality} (f-orthogonality) of
  a cycle \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) \emph{to} a cycle  \({\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) is
  defined by the condition that the cycle \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}
  {\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} { C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) is orthogonal (in the
  sense of Definition~\ref{de:orthogonality-first}) to the real line,
  i.e is a self-adjoint cycle in the sense of
  Definition~\ref{de:self-adj-cycle}. Analytically this is defined by
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:f-orthog-def}
    \Re\mathop{tr}({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} {\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}{ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} R^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}})=0
  \end{equation}
  and  we denote it by \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} \dashv   {\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\).
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- remark-17: body_md -->
\label{re:real-line-inv-3}
  This definition is explicitly based on the invariance of the real
  line and is an illustration to the boundary value effect from
  Rem.~\ref{re:real-line-inv-0}.
<!-- end remark-17 -->
<!-- remark-18: body_md -->
It is easy to observe the following
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item f-orthogonality is not a symmetric: \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} \dashv
  {\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) does not implies \({\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} \dashv
  { C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\);
  \item 
    \label{it:s-orth-sl2-inv}
    Since the real axis \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}}\) and
    orthogonality~\eqref{eq:orthogonality-first} are \(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\)-invariant
    objects f-orthogonality is also \(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\)-invariant.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-18 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
The image \({ C^{s_1}_{\breve{\sigma}}}  R^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}} { C^{s_1}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) of the
  real line under inversion in \({ C^{s_1}_{\breve{\sigma}}}=(k,l,n,m)\) is the cycle:
  \begin{displaymath}
    (2 s s_1 \breve{\sigma} k n,\ 2 s s_1 \breve{\sigma} l n,\ s^2 (l^2+\breve{\sigma} n^2-m k),\ 2 s s_1 \breve{\sigma} m n).
  \end{displaymath}
  It is the real line if \(s\cdot\det({ C^{s_1}_{\breve{\sigma}}})\neq0\) and   either
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item  \(s_1 n=0\), in this case it is a composition of \(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\)-action by \(
    \begin{pmatrix}
      l&-me_0\\ke_0 &-l
    \end{pmatrix}\) and the reflection in the real line; or
  \item  \(\breve{\sigma}=0\), i.e. the parabolic case of the cycle space.
  \end{enumerate}
  If this condition is satisfied than f-orthogonality
  preserved by the inversion \({\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\rightarrow { C^{s_1}_{\breve{\sigma}}} {\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}
  { C^{s_1}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) in \({\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\).
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
f-orthogonality of \({{ C^{s}_{p}}}\) to
  \({{\tilde C^{s}_{p}}}\) is given by either of the following
  equivalent identities
  \begin{eqnarray*}
                                                                     
                                                   
     \tilde{n} (l^{2}-\breve{e}_1^2 n^{2}- m k) + \tilde{m} n k-2\tilde{l}
     n l+ \tilde{k} m n & =& 0, \qquad \textrm{ or} \\
                                                                                         
     \tilde{n} \det({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}) + n\left\langle { C^{s}_{p}},{\tilde C^{s}_{p}} 
        \right\rangle\ifx\relax\relax\else_{\relax}\fi & =& 0. 
  \end{eqnarray*}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
This is another \textsf{GiNaC}\ calculation~\cite{Kisil05b}*{\S~\ref{G-sec:expr-orth-s.k}}
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{pr:focal-ortho}
  Let \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) be a cycle, then its \emph{f-ghost cycle}
  \({\tilde C^{\breve{\sigma}}_{\breve{\sigma}}} = { C^{\chi(\sigma)}_{\breve{\sigma}}}
  \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{\breve{\sigma}}_{\breve{\sigma}}{}} { C^{\chi(\sigma)}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) is the reflection of
  the real line in \({ C^{\chi(\sigma)}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\), where
  \(\chi(\sigma)\) is the \emph{Heaviside function}~\ref{eq:heaviside-function}.
  Then
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item Cycles \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) and \({\tilde C^{\breve{\sigma}}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\)
    have the same roots.
  \item \label{item:focal-centre-rel}
    \(\chi(\sigma)\)-Centre of \({\tilde C^{\breve{\sigma}}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) coincides with the \(\breve{\sigma}\)-focus of
    \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\), consequently all lines f-orthogonal to
    \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) are passing one of its foci.
  \item s-Reflection in \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) defined from
    f-orthogonality (see
    Definition~\ref{def:inversion}.\ref{item:inversion-orthogonality}) coincides with
    usual inversion in \({\tilde C^{\breve{\sigma}}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
This again is calculated in \textsf{GiNaC}, see~\cite{Kisil05b}*{\S~\ref{G-sec:invers-from-orth}}.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
\label{de:radius}
  The \(\breve{\sigma}\)-\emph{radius} of a cycle \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) if squared is equal
  to the \(\breve{\sigma}\)-determinant of cycle's \(k\)-normalised (see
  Defn.~\ref{de:normalisation}) matrix, i.e.
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:radius}
    r^2= \frac{\det{ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}}{k^2} =\frac{l^2- \breve{\sigma} n^{2}-km}{k^2}.
  \end{equation}
  As usual, the \(\breve{\sigma}\)-\emph{diameter} of a cycles is two times its radius.
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
The \(\breve{\sigma}\)-\emph{radius} of a cycle \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) is equal to
  \(1/k\), where \(k\) is \((2,1)\)-entry of \(\det\)-normalised
  matrix (see Defn.~\ref{de:normalisation}) of the cycle.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- remark-19: body_md -->
Note that
  \begin{displaymath}
    r^2_{\breve{\sigma}}=-4*f*u_{\breve{\sigma}},    
  \end{displaymath}
  where \(r^2_{\breve{\sigma}}\) is the square of cycle's \(\breve{\sigma}\)-radius,
  \(u_{\breve{\sigma}}\) is the second coordinate of its \(\breve{\sigma}\)-focus and \(f\)
  its focal length.
<!-- end remark-19 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
\label{de:distance}
  The \((\sigma,\breve{\sigma})\)-\emph{distance} between two points is the extremum of
  \(\breve{\sigma}\)-dia\-me\-ters for all \(\sigma\)-cycles passing through both points.
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
\label{de:length}
  The \(\breve{\sigma}\)-\emph{length} from a \(\mathring{\sigma}\)-centre or from a \(\mathring{\sigma}\)-focus
  of a directed interval \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) is the \(\breve{\sigma}\)-radius of the
  \(\sigma\)-cycle with its \(\mathring{\sigma}\)-\emph{centre} or
  \(\mathring{\sigma}\)-\emph{focus} correspondingly at the point \(A\) which passes
  through \(B\). These lengths are denoted by \(l_c(\overrightarrow{AB})\) and
  \(l_f(\overrightarrow{AB})\) correspondingly.
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- remark-20: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Note that the distance is a symmetric functions of two points
    by its definition and this is not necessarily true for
    lengths. For modal logic of non-symmetric distances
    see, for example, \cite{KuruczWolterZakharyaschev05}. However the
    first axiom (\(l(x,y)=0\) iff  \(x=y\)) should be modified as follows:
    \begin{displaymath}
     ( l(x,y)=0 \text{ and } l(x,y)=0 ) \text{ iff } x=y.
    \end{displaymath}
  \item A cycle is uniquely defined by elliptic or hyperbolic centre
    and a point which it passes. However the parabolic centre is not
    so useful. Correspondingly \((\sigma,0)\)-length from parabolic
    centre is not properly defined. 
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-20 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{le:distance-first} 
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item The cycle of the form~\eqref{eq:zero-cycle-matrix} has zero
  radius. 
  \item The distance between two points \(y=e_0u+e_1v\)
       and  \(y'=e_0u'+e_1v'\) in the elliptic or hyperbolic spaces is
    \begin{equation}
      \label{eq:distance-first-ell-hyp}
      d^2(y, y') = \frac{ \breve{\sigma} ((u-u')^2-\sigma(v- v')^2) +4(1-\sigma\breve{\sigma}) v v'}
      {(u- u')^2 \breve{\sigma}-(v-v')^2} ((u-u')^2 -\sigma(v- v')^2),
    \end{equation}
    and in parabolic case it is (see Fig.~\ref{fig:distances}(b)
    and~\cite{Yaglom79}*{p.~38, (5)}) 
    \begin{equation}
      \label{eq:distance-first-par}
      d^2(y, y') = (u-u')^2.
    \end{equation}
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Let \({ C^{\sigma}_{s}}(l)\) be the family of cycles passing through
  both points \((u, v)\) and \((u', v')\) (under the assumption
  \(v\neq v'\)) and parametrised by its coefficient \(l\) in the
  defining equation~\eqref{eq:cycle-def}.  By a calculation done in
  \textsf{GiNaC}~\cite{Kisil05b}*{\S~\ref{G-sec:dist-betw-points}} we found
  that the only critical point of \(\det({ C^{\sigma}_{s}}(l))\) is:
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:critical-point}
    l_0 = 
                
                                                                                         
                              
    \frac{1}{2}\left((u'+u) +
    (\breve{\sigma}\sigma-1)\frac{(u'-u)(v^2-v'^2)}
    {(u'- u)^2 \breve{\sigma}-(v-v')^2} \right),
  \end{equation}
  [Note that in the case \(\sigma\breve{\sigma}=1\), i.e. both points and cycles
  spaces are simultaneously either elliptic or hyperbolic, this
  expression reduces to the expected midpoint
  \(l_0=\frac{1}{2}(u+u')\).] Since in the elliptic or hyperbolic case
  the parameter \(l\) can take any real value, the extremum of
  \(\det({ C^{\sigma}_{s}}(l))\) is reached in \(l_0\) and is equal
  to~\eqref{eq:distance-first-ell-hyp} (calculated by
  \textsf{GiNaC}~\cite{Kisil05b}*{\S~\ref{G-sec:dist-betw-points}}). A separate
  calculation for the case \(v= v'\) gives the same answer.

  In the parabolic case the possible values of \(l\) are either in
  \((-\infty, \frac{1}{2}(u+u'))\), or \((\frac{1}{2}(u+u'),\infty)\),
  or the only value is \(l=\frac{1}{2}(u+u')\) since for that value a
  parabola should flip between upward and downward directions of its
  branches. In any of those cases the extremum value corresponds to the
  boundary point \(l=\frac{1}{2}(u+u')\) and is equal
  to~\eqref{eq:distance-first-par}.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{co:inner-product-dist}
  If cycles \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) and \({\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) are
  normalised by conditions \(k=1\) and \(\tilde{k}=1\) then
  \begin{displaymath}
    \left\langle { C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}},{\tilde C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} 
        \right\rangle\ifx\relax\relax\else_{\relax}\fi =
    \left| c-\tilde{c} \right|\ifx\relax\relax\else_{\relax}\fi_{\breve{\sigma}}^2-r_{\breve{\sigma}}^2-\tilde{r}_{\breve{\sigma}}^2, 
  \end{displaymath}
  where  \(\left| c-c \right|\ifx\relax\relax\else_{\relax}\fi_{\breve{\sigma}}^2=(l-\tilde{l})^2-\breve{\sigma}(n-\tilde{n})^2\) is
  the square of \(\breve{\sigma}\)-distance between cycles' centres,
  \(r_{\breve{\sigma}}\) and \(\tilde{r}_{\breve{\sigma}}\) are \(bs\)-radii of the
  respective cycles.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- remark-21: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
  \item In the three cases \(\sigma=\breve{\sigma}=-1\), \(0\) or \(1\), which
    were typically studied before, the above distances are conveniently defined
    through the Clifford algebra multiplications
    \begin{displaymath}
      d_{e,p,h}^2(ue_0+ve_1)=-(ue_0+ve_1)^2.    
    \end{displaymath}
  \item Unless \(\sigma=\breve{\sigma}\) the parabolic
    distance~\eqref{eq:distance-first-par} is not received
    from~\eqref{eq:distance-first-ell-hyp} by the substitution
    \(\sigma =0\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-21 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{le:distance-second}
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \label{it:length-centre}
    The \(\breve{\sigma}\)-length from the \(\mathring{\sigma}\)-centre between two
    points \(y=e_0u+e_1v\) and \(y'=e_0u'+e_1v'\) is
    \begin{equation}
      \label{eq:k-center-point}
      l_{c_{\breve{\sigma}}}^2(y, y')   =  
 (u-u')^2-\sigma v'^2+2\mathring{\sigma} v v' -\breve{\sigma} v^2.
                                                          
                                                                          
    \end{equation}
  \item \label{it:length-focus}
    The \(\breve{\sigma}\)-length from the \(\mathring{\sigma}\)-focus between two
    points \(y=e_0u+e_1v\) and \(y'=e_0u'+e_1v'\) is
    \begin{equation}
      \label{eq:k-focus-point}
      l_{f_{\breve{\sigma}}}^2(y, y')  = (\mathring{\sigma}-\breve{\sigma}) p^2-2vp,
    \end{equation}
    where:
    \begin{eqnarray}
      \label{eq:focal-length}
      p & = & \mathring{\sigma}\left(-(v'-v)\pm\sqrt{\mathring{\sigma}(u'-u)^2+(v'-v)^2-\sigma\mathring{\sigma}
          v'^2}\right), \quad\text{if } \mathring{\sigma}\neq0;\\
      \label{eq:parab-focal-length}
      p & = & \frac{(u'-u)^2-\sigma v'^2}{2(v'-v)}, \quad\text{if } \mathring{\sigma}=0.
    \end{eqnarray}
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Identity~\eqref{eq:k-center-point} is verified in
  \textsf{GiNaC}~\cite{Kisil05b}*{\S~\ref{G-sec:length-direct-interv}}. For the
  second part we observe that the parabola with the focus \((u,v)\)
  passing through \((u',v')\) has the following parameters:
  \begin{displaymath}
   k=1,\quad l= u,\quad n=p,\quad  m = 2\mathring{\sigma} pv'-u'^2+2uu'+\sigma v'^2.
  \end{displaymath}
  Then the formula~\eqref{eq:k-focus-point} is verified by the \textsf{GiNaC}\
  calculation~\cite{Kisil05b}*{\S~\ref{G-sec:length-interv-from}}.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- remark-22: body_md -->
\label{re:focal-lenght}
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item     The value of  \(p\) in~\eqref{eq:focal-length} is the
    focal length of either of the two cycles, which are in the 
    parabolic case upward or downward parabolas (corresponding to the
    plus or minus signs) with focus at \((u, v)\) and passing through
    \((u', v')\).
  \item \label{it:more-lengths}
    In the case \(\sigma\breve{\sigma}=1\) the
    length~\eqref{eq:k-center-point} became the standard elliptic
    or hyperbolic distance \((u-u')^2-\sigma (v-v')^2\) obtained
    in~\eqref{eq:distance-first-ell-hyp}. Since these expressions
    appeared both as distances and lengths they are widely used. 

    On the other hand in the parabolic
    space we get three additional lengths besides of
    distance~\eqref{eq:distance-first-par}:   
    \begin{displaymath}
      l_{c_{\breve{\sigma}}}^2(y, y')    =  (u-u')^2+2 v v'-\breve{\sigma} v^2
    \end{displaymath}
    parametrised by \(\breve{\sigma}\) (cf.~Remark~\ref{rem:prejudice}.\ref{it:par-is-zero}). 
  \item The parabolic distance~\eqref{eq:distance-first-par} can
    be expressed as 
    \begin{displaymath}
      d^2(y, y') = p^2+2(v-v')p
    \end{displaymath}
    in terms of the focal length~\eqref{eq:focal-length}, which is an
    expression similar to~\eqref{eq:k-focus-point}.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-22 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
\label{de:conformal}
  We say that a distance or a length \(d\) is \(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\)-\emph{conformal} if for
  fixed \(y\), \(y'\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{\sigma}_{}{}}\) the limit:
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:conformal-lim}
    \lim_{t\rightarrow 0} \frac{d(g\cdot y, g\cdot(y+ty'))}{d(y,
      y+ty')}, \qquad
    \text{ where } g\in\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}, 
  \end{equation}
  exists and its value depends only from \(y\) and \(g\) and is
  independent from \(y'\).
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{pr:conformity}
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \label{it:conformity-dist}
    The distance~\eqref{eq:distance-first-ell-hyp} is conformal if
    and only if the type of point and cycle spaces are the same, i.e.
    \(\sigma\breve{\sigma}=1\). The parabolic
    distance~\eqref{eq:distance-first-par} is conformal only in the
    parabolic point space.
  \item \label{it:conformity-length-centre}
    The lengths from centres~\eqref{eq:k-center-point} are
    conformal for any combination of values of \(\sigma\),
    \(\breve{\sigma}\)  and \(\mathring{\sigma}\). 
  \item \label{it:conformity-length-foci} The lengths from
    foci~\eqref{eq:k-focus-point} are conformal for \(\mathring{\sigma}\neq 0\) and
    any combination of values of \(\sigma\) and \(\breve{\sigma}\).
                         
                                                         
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
This is another straightforward calculation in
  \textsf{GiNaC}~\cite{Kisil05b}*{\S~\ref{G-sec:check-conformity}}.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{pr:parab-conf}
  Let the focal length is given by the
  identity~\eqref{eq:k-focus-point}  with \(\sigma=\mathring{\sigma}=0\), e.g.:
  \begin{displaymath}
    l_{f_{\breve{\sigma}}}^2(y, y')  = -\breve{\sigma} p^2-2vp, \qquad \text{where}
    \quad
    p = \frac{(u'-u)^2             
    }{2(v'-v)}
  \end{displaymath}
  Then it is conformal in the sense that for any constant \(y=ue_0+ve_1\)
  and \(y'=u'e_0+v'e_1\) with a fixed \(u'\) we have:
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:parab-conf-factor}
    \lim_{v'\rightarrow \infty} \frac{l_{f_{\breve{\sigma}}}(g\cdot y,
      g\cdot y')}{l_{f_{\breve{\sigma}}}(y, y')}
    =\frac{1}{(cu+d)^2},\qquad \text{where}\quad
    g=
    \begin{pmatrix}
      a&be_0\\-ce_0&d
    \end{pmatrix}.
  \end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- remark-23: body_md -->
The expressions of
  lengths~\eqref{eq:k-center-point}--\eqref{eq:k-focus-point} are
  generally non-symmetric and this is a price one should pay for its
  non-triviality. All symmetric distances lead to nine two-dimensional
  Cayley-Klein geometries, see~\citelist{\cite{Yaglom79}*{App.~B}
  \cite{HerranzSantander02a} \cite{HerranzSantander02b}}. In the parabolic
  case a symmetric distance of a vector \((u,v)\) is always a function
  of \(u\) alone, cf. Rem.~\ref{re:par-is-not-limit}. For such a
  distance a parabolic unit circle consists from two vertical lines
  (see dotted vertical lines in the second rows on
  Figs.~\ref{fig:orthogonality1} and~\ref{fig:orthogonality2}), which
  is not aesthetically attractive. On the other hand the parabolic
  ``unit cycles'' defined by lengths~\eqref{eq:k-center-point}
  and~\eqref{eq:k-focus-point} are parabolas, which makes the parabolic
  Cayley transform (see Section~\ref{sec:parab-cayl-transf}) very
  natural.
<!-- end remark-23 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
Let the line element be \(\left| dy \right|\ifx\relax\relax\else_{\relax}\fi^2=du^2-\sigma dv^2\) and
  the ``length of a curve'' is given by the corresponding line
  integral, cf.~\cite{Beardon05a}*{\S~15.2}: 
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:curve-length}
    \int_\Gamma \frac{\left| dy \right|\ifx\relax\relax\else_{\relax}\fi}{v}.
  \end{equation}
  Then the length of the curve is preserved under the M\"obius
  transformations.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
The proof is based on the following three observations:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item The line element \(\left| dy \right|\ifx\relax\relax\else_{\relax}\fi^2=du^2-\sigma dv^2\) at the point \(e_1\)
    is invariant under action of the respective fix-group of this
    point (see Lem.~\ref{le:fix-subgroups}).
  \item The fraction \(\frac{\left| dy \right|\ifx\relax\relax\else_{\relax}\fi}{v}\) is invariant under
    action of the \(ax+b\)-group.
  \item M\"obius action of \(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\) in each EPH case is generated by
    \(ax+b\) group and the corresponding fix-subgroup, see
    Lem.~\ref{le:fix-ax+b-gen-sl2}. 
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
Let two points \(w_1\) and \(w_2\) in the upper half-plane are
  linked by an arc of a parabola with zero \(\breve{\sigma}\)-radius. Then the
  length~\eqref{eq:curve-length} along the arc is invariant under
  M\"obius transformations.
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
\label{de:perpendicular}
  Let \(l\) be a length or distance.  We say that a vector \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) is
  \emph{\(l\)-perpendicular} to a vector \(\overrightarrow{CD}\) if function
  \(l(\overrightarrow{AB}+\varepsilon \overrightarrow{CD})\) of a variable \(\varepsilon\) has a
  local extremum at \(\varepsilon=0\). This is denoted by
  \(\overrightarrow{AB}\leftthreetimes \overrightarrow{CD}\).
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- remark-24: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Obviously the \(l\)-perpendicularity is not a symmetric notion
    (i.e. \(\overrightarrow{AB}\leftthreetimes \overrightarrow{CD}\) does not imply
    \(\overrightarrow{CD}\leftthreetimes \overrightarrow{AB}\)) similarly to
    f-orthogonality, see subsection~\ref{sec:focal-orthogonality}.
  \item \(l\)-perpendicularity is obviously linear in  \(\overrightarrow{CD}\),
    i.e.  \(\overrightarrow{AB}\leftthreetimes \overrightarrow{CD}\) implies
    \(\overrightarrow{AB}\leftthreetimes r\overrightarrow{CD}\) for any real non-zero
    \(r\). However \(l\)-perpendicularity is not generally linear in
    \(\overrightarrow{AB}\), i.e. \(\overrightarrow{AB}\leftthreetimes \overrightarrow{CD}\) does
    not necessarily imply \(r\overrightarrow{AB}\leftthreetimes \overrightarrow{CD}\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-24 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{le:parp-ortho}
  Let \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) be \(l_{c_{\breve{\sigma}}}\)-perpendicular
  (\(l_{f_{\breve{\sigma}}}\)-perpendicular) to a vector \(\overrightarrow{CD}\). Then the
  flat cycle (straight line) \(AB\), is (s-)orthogonal to the cycle
  \({ C^{s}_{\sigma}}\) with centre (focus) at \(A\) passing through
  \(B\). The vector \(\overrightarrow{CD}\) is tangent to \({ C^{s}_{\sigma}}\)
  at \(B\).
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
This follows from the relation of centre of (s-)ghost cycle to
  centre (focus) of (s-)orthogonal cycle stated in
  Props.~\ref{pr:ghost-cycle} and~\ref{pr:focal-ortho}
  correspondingly.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{le:perp-explicit}  
  Let \(A=(u,v)\) and \(B=(u',v')\). Then
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \(d\)-perpendicular (in the sense
    of~\eqref{eq:distance-first-ell-hyp}) to \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) in the
    \emph{elliptic} or \emph{hyperbolic} cases is a multiple of the vector
    \begin{displaymath}
      (\sigma (v-v')^3-(u-u')^2 (v+v'(1-2 \sigma \breve{\sigma})), \breve{\sigma}(u-u')^3-(u-u')(v- v')(-2 v' +(v+v')
      \breve{\sigma} \sigma)),    
    \end{displaymath}
    which for \(\sigma\breve{\sigma}=1\) reduces to the expected
    value \((v-v', \sigma(u-u'))\).
  \item \label{it:d-perp-parab} \(d\)-perpendicular (in the sense
    of~\eqref{eq:distance-first-par}) to \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) in the
    \emph{parabolic} case is \((0, t)\), \(t\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}}\) which
    coincides with the \emph{Galilean orthogonality} defined
    in~\textup{\cite{Yaglom79}*{\S~3}}.
  \item \(l_{c_{\breve{\sigma}}}\)-perpendicular (in the sense
    of~\eqref{eq:k-center-point}) to \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) is a multiple of
                
    \((\sigma v'-\mathring{\sigma} v, u-u')\).
  \item \label{it:focal-perpendicularity}
    \(l_{f_{\breve{\sigma}}}\)-perpendicular (in the sense
    of~\eqref{eq:k-focus-point}) to \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) is a multiple of
                 
    \((\sigma v'+p, u-u')\), where \(p\) is defined
    either by~\eqref{eq:focal-length} or
    by~\eqref{eq:parab-focal-length} for corresponding values of
    \(\mathring{\sigma}\). 
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
The perpendiculars are calculated by
  \textsf{GiNaC}~\cite{Kisil05b}*{\S~\ref{G-sec:calc-perp}}.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{lem:orthogonal1}
  Let \(\overrightarrow{AB}=u e_0+v e_1\) and
  \(\overrightarrow{CD}=u'e_0+v'e_1\), then:
  \begin{enumerate} 
    \renewcommand{(\ifcase\csname c@enumi\endcsname a\or e\or p\or h\fi)}{(\ifcase\csname c@enumi\endcsname a\or e\or p\or h\fi)}
  \item \label{it:ell-perpendic}
    In the elliptic case the \(d\)-perpendicularity for \(\breve{\sigma}=-1\)
    means that \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) and \(\overrightarrow{CD}\) form a right angle, or
    analytically \(u u'+v v'=0\).
  \item \label{item:par-orthogon} In the parabolic case
    the \(l_{f_{\breve{\sigma}}}\)-perpendicularity for \(\breve{\sigma}=1\) means that
    \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) bisect the angle between \(\overrightarrow{CD}\) and the
    vertical direction or analytically:
    \begin{equation}
      \label{eq:par-s-perp}
      u'u-v'p=u'u-v'(\sqrt{u^2+v^2}-v)=0,
    \end{equation}
    where \(p\) is the focal length~\eqref{eq:focal-length}
  \item In the hyperbolic case the \(d\)-perpendicularity for
    \(\breve{\sigma}=-1\) means that the angles between \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) and
    \(\overrightarrow{CD}\) are bisected by lines parallel to \(u=\pm v\), or
    analytically \(u' u-v' v=0\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- remark-25: body_md -->
\label{re:par-is-not-limit}
  If one attempts to devise a parabolic length as a limit or an
  intermediate case for the elliptic \(l_e=u^2+v^2\) and hyperbolic
  \(l_p=u^2-v^2\) lengths then the only possible guess is
  \(l'_p=u^2\)~\eqref{eq:distance-first-par}, which is too trivial for
  an interesting geometry.
  
  Similarly the only orthogonality conditions linking the
  elliptic \(u_1 u_2+v_1 v_2=0\) and the hyperbolic \(u_1 u_2-v_1
  v_2=0\) cases seems to be \(u_1 u_2=0\) (see~\cite{Yaglom79}*{\S~3}
  and Lem.~\ref{le:perp-explicit}.\ref{it:d-perp-parab}), which is again too trivial.  This
  support our Remark~\ref{rem:prejudice}.\ref{it:par-is-limit}.
<!-- end remark-25 -->
<!-- definition-17: body_md -->
A cycle \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) such that \(\det{ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) is an
  infinitesimal number is called
  \emph{infinitesimal radius cycle}.
<!-- end definition-17 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
Let \(\breve{\sigma}\) and \(\mathring{\sigma}\) be two metric signs and let a point
  \((u_0,v_0)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{p}_{}{}}\) with \(v_0>0\).  Consider a cycle
  \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) defined by
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:inf-cycle}
    { C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}=(1, u_0, n, u_0^2+2 n v_0
    -\mathring{\sigma} n^2),
  \end{equation}
  where
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:inf-cycle-n-value}
    n=\left\{
      \begin{array}{ll}
        \displaystyle    \frac{v_0-\sqrt{v_0^2-(\mathring{\sigma}-\breve{\sigma})\varepsilon^2}}{\mathring{\sigma}-\breve{\sigma}},&\text{ if } \mathring{\sigma}\neq \breve{\sigma};\\
       \displaystyle \frac{\varepsilon^2}{2v_0},&\text{ if } \mathring{\sigma}=\breve{\sigma}.
      \end{array}\right.
  \end{equation}
  Then 
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item The point \((u_0, v_0)\) is \(\mathring{\sigma}\)-focus of the cycle.
  \item The square of \(\breve{\sigma}\)-radius is exactly \(-\varepsilon^2\),
    i.e.~\eqref{eq:inf-cycle} defines an infinitesimal radius cycle. 
  \item The focal length of the cycle is an infinitesimal
    number of order \(\varepsilon^2\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
The cycle~\eqref{eq:inf-cycle} has the squared \(\breve{\sigma}\)-radius equal
  to \(-\varepsilon^2\) if \(n\) is a root to the equation:
  \begin{displaymath}
    (\mathring{\sigma}-\breve{\sigma})n^2-2v_0n+\varepsilon^2=0.
  \end{displaymath}
  Moreover only the root from~\eqref{eq:inf-cycle-n-value} of the
  quadratic case gives an infinitesimal focal length.  This also is
  supported by calculations done in \textsf{GiNaC},
  see~\cite{Kisil05b}*{\S~\ref{G-sec:basic-prop-infin}}.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
{\cite{Kisil05b}*{\S~\ref{G-sec:basic-prop-infin}}}
  Infinitesimal cycle~\eqref{eq:inf-cycle} consists of points, which are infinitesimally
  close (in the sense of length from focus~\eqref{eq:k-focus-point})
  to  its focus \(F=(u_0, v_0)\):
  \begin{equation}
    \label{eq:inf-cycle-points}
                                                                       
    (u_0+\varepsilon u, v_0+v_0u^2+((\breve{\sigma}-\mathring{\sigma}) u^2-\mathring{\sigma})
    \frac{\varepsilon^2}{4v_0}+O(\varepsilon^3)).
  \end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
<!-- lemma-26: body_md -->
\label{le:infinites-cycle-inv}
  The image of \(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\)-action on an infinitesimal radius
  cycle~\eqref{eq:inf-cycle} by
  conjugation~\eqref{eq:cycle-transform-short} is an infinitesimal
  radius cycle of the same order. 

  Image of an infinitesimal cycle under cycle conjugation is an
  infinitesimal cycle of the same or lesser order.
<!-- end lemma-26 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
These are calculations done in \textsf{GiNaC},
  see~\cite{Kisil05b}*{\S~\ref{G-sec:mobi-transf-infin}}.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- lemma-27: body_md -->
\label{le:infinitesimal-ortho} 
  Let \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) be the
  infinitesimal cycle~\eqref{eq:inf-cycle} and \({\breve C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}=(k,l,n,m)\) be a
  generic cycle. Then
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item The orthogonality condition~\eqref{eq:orthogonality-first}
    \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\perp {\breve C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) and the
    f-orthogonality~\eqref{eq:f-orthog-def} \({\breve C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}
    \dashv { C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) both are given by:
    \begin{displaymath}
      ku_0^2-2lu_0+m=O(\varepsilon).
    \end{displaymath}
    In other words the cycle \({\breve C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) has root
    \(u_0\) in the parabolic space. 
  \item \label{it:infinitesimal-f-ortho}
    The f-orthogonality~\eqref{eq:f-orthog-def} \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}
    \dashv {\breve C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) is given by:
    \begin{equation}
      \label{eq:f-orthog-infinites}
      ku_0^2-2lu_0-2nv_0+m=O(\varepsilon).
    \end{equation}
    In other words the cycle \({\breve C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) passes focus
    \((u_0,v_0)\) of the infinitesimal cycle in the parabolic space. 
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-27 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
These are \textsf{GiNaC}\ calculations~\cite{Kisil05b}*{\S~\ref{G-sec:orth-with-infin}}.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- definition-18: body_md -->
\label{de:infinites-conform}
  A map of a region of \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{a}_{}{}}\) to another region is
  \(l\)-infinitesimally conformal for a length \(l\) (in the sense of
  Defn.~\ref{de:length}) if for any \(l\)-infinitesimal cycle: 
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item Its image is an \(l\)-infinitesimal cycle of the same order;
  \item The image of its centre/focus is displaced from the centre/focus of its
    image by an infinitesimal number of a greater order than its radius.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-18 -->
<!-- remark-26: body_md -->
Note that in comparison with Defn.~\ref{de:conformal} we now work
  ``in the opposite direction'': former we had the fixed group of
  motions and looked for corresponding conformal lengths/distances,
  now we take a distance/length (encoded in the infinitesimally equidistant
  cycle) and check which motions respect it.
<!-- end remark-26 -->
<!-- proposition-11: body_md -->
\label{pr:infinit-conf}
  Let \({\breve C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) be the image under \(g\in\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\) of an infinitesimal
  cycle \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) from~\eqref{eq:inf-cycle}.
  Then \(\mathring{\sigma}\)-focus of \({\breve C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) is  displaced from
  \(g(u_0,v_0)\) by infinitesimals of order \(\varepsilon^2\) (while
  both cycles have \(\breve{\sigma}\)-radius of order \(\varepsilon\)).

  Consequently \(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\)-action is infinitesimally conformal in the
  sense of Defn.~\ref{de:infinites-conform} with
  respect to the length from focus (Defn.~\ref{de:length}) for all
  combinations of \(\sigma\), \(\breve{\sigma}\) and \(\mathring{\sigma}\).
<!-- end proposition-11 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
These are \textsf{GiNaC}\ calculations~\cite{Kisil05b}*{\S~\ref{G-sec:mobi-transf-infin}}.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- remark-27: body_md -->
\label{re:non-standard}
  There is another connection between parabolic function theory and
  non-standard analysis. As was mentioned in
  \S~\ref{sec:ellipt-parab-hyperb}, the Clifford algebra \({\ensuremath{ 
\mathcal{C}\kern-0.12em\ell(p)}}\)
  corresponds to the set of \emph{dual numbers} \(u+\varepsilon v\)
  with \(\varepsilon^2=0\)~\cite{Yaglom79}*{Supl.~C}. On the other hand
  we may consider the set of numbers \(u+\varepsilon v\) within the
  non-standard analysis, with \(\varepsilon\) being an infinitesimal.
  In this case \(\varepsilon^2\) is a higher order infinitesimal than
  \(\varepsilon\) and effectively can be treated as \(0\) at
  infinitesimal scale of \(\varepsilon\), i.e. we again get the dual
  numbers condition \(\varepsilon^2=0\). This explains why many results
  of differential calculus can be naturally deduced within dual numbers
