  framework~\cite{CatoniCannataNichelatti04}.
<!-- end remark-27 -->
<!-- definition-19: body_md -->
The only irregular point \((0,0,0,1)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}^{3}_{}{}}\) of the map
  \(Q\) is called \emph{zero-radius cycle at infinity} and denoted by
  \( Z^{}_{\infty}\).
<!-- end definition-19 -->
<!-- lemma-28: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \( Z^{}_{\infty}\) is the image of the zero-radius cycle
    \( Z^{}_{(0,0)}=(1,0,0,0)\) at the origin under reflection
    (inversion) into the unit cycle \((1, 0,0,-1)\), see blue cycles
    in Fig.~\ref{fig:inversions}(b)-(d).
  \item The following statements are equivalent
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item A point \((u,v)\in\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{\sigma}_{}{}}\) belongs to the
      zero-radius cycle \( Z^{}_{(0,0)}\) centred at the origin;
     \item The zero-radius cycle \( Z^{}_{(u,v)}\) is \(\sigma\)-orthogonal to 
      zero-radius cycle \( Z^{}_{(0,0)}\);
    \item The inversion \(z\mapsto \frac{1}{z}\) in the unit cycle is
      singular in the point \((u,v)\);
    \item The image of \( Z^{}_{(u,v)}\) under inversion in the unit
      cycle is orthogonal to  \( Z^{}_{\infty}\). 
    \end{enumerate}
    If any from the above is true we also say that image of \((u,v)\) under
    inversion in the unit cycle belongs to zero-radius cycle at infinity.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-28 -->
<!-- lemma-29: body_md -->
In the elliptic and parabolic cases the upper halfplane in
  \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{\sigma}_{}{}}\) is preserved by M\"obius transformations from
  \(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\). However in the hyperbolic case any point \((u,v)\) with
  \(v>0\) can be mapped to an arbitrary point \((u',v')\) with
  \(v'\neq 0\).
<!-- end lemma-29 -->
<!-- remark-28: body_md -->
\label{rem:two-cver}
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \label{it:hyp-object} The hyperbolic orbit of the \(K\)
    subgroup in the \(\ensuremath{ { \widetilde{\mathbb{R}}^{h}} }\) consists of two branches of the
    hyperbola passing through \((0,v)\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{h}_{+}{}}\) and
    \((0,-v^{-1})\) in \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{h}_{-}{}}\), see
    Fig.~\ref{fig:hyp-upper-half-plane}.  If we watch the rotation of
    a straight line generating a cone~\eqref{eq:cones-fam} then its
    intersection with the plane \(HH'\) on
    Fig.~\ref{fig:k-orbit-sect}(d) will draw the both branches. 
    As mentioned in Rem.~\ref{rem:orbits2}.\ref{it:hyp-orbit} they have the same
    focal length.
  \item The ``upper'' halfplane is bounded by two disjoint ``real''
    axes denoted by \(AA'\) and \(C'C''\) in
    Fig.~\ref{fig:hyp-upper-half-plane}.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-28 -->
<!-- lemma-30: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
  \item In the \emph{elliptic case} the ``real axis'' \(U\) is transformed
    to the unit circle and the upper half-plane---to the unit disk: 
    \begin{eqnarray}
      \label{eq:unit-circle-ell}
      \{(u,v) \,\mid\, v = 0\} &\to& \{ (u',v') \,\mid\, l^2_{c_e}(u'e_0+v'e_1)= u'^2+v'^2=1\} \\
      \label{eq:unit-disk-ell}
      \{(u,v) \,\mid\, v > 0\} &\to& \{(u',v') \,\mid\,
      l^2_{c_e}(u'e_0+v'e_1)= u'^2+v'^2<1\},
    \end{eqnarray}
    where the length from centre \(l^2_{c_e}\) is given
    by~\eqref{eq:k-center-point} for \(\sigma=\breve{\sigma}=-1\).

    On both sets \(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\) acts transitively and the unit circle is generated,
    for example, by the point \((0, 1)\) and the unit disk is generated by
    \((0,0)\). 
  \item In the \emph{hyperbolic case} the ``real axis'' \(U\) is transformed
    to the hyperbolic unit circle: 
    \begin{equation}
      \label{eq:unit-circle-hyp}
      \{(u,v) \,\mid\, v = 0\} \to \{ (u',v') \,\mid\, l^2_{c_h}(u',v')= u'^2-v'^2=-1\}, 
    \end{equation}
    where the length from centre \(l^2_{c_h}\) is given
    by~\eqref{eq:k-center-point} for \(\sigma=\breve{\sigma}=1\).

    On the  hyperbolic unit circle \(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\) acts transitively and it is
    generated, for example, by point \((0,1)\). 

    \(\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\ifxSLl \ell_{2}^{}{}\else
  SL_{2}^{}{}\fi}(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{}_{}{}})}\) acts also \emph{transitively on the whole complement}
    \begin{displaymath}
      \{(u',v') \,\mid\, l^2_{c_h}(u'e_0+v'e_1)\neq -1\}
    \end{displaymath}
    to the unit circle, i.e. on its ``inner'' and ``outer'' parts
    together.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-30 -->
<!-- lemma-31: body_md -->
\label{le:parabolic-disk}
  Parabolic Cayley transform \(P_{\breve{\sigma}}\) as defined by the matrix
  \(C_{\breve{\sigma}}\)~\eqref{eq:parab-cayley-matr} acts on the \(V\)-axis
  always as a shift one unit down.

  Its image can be described in term of various lengths as follows:
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \label{it:parab-unit-disk-cen} \(P_{\breve{\sigma}}\) for \(\breve{\sigma}\neq0\)
      transforms the ``real axis'' \(U\) to the p-cycle with the
      p-length squared \(-\breve{\sigma}\) from its e-centre
      \((0,-\frac{\breve{\sigma}}{2})\), cf.~\eqref{eq:unit-circle-ell}:
    \begin{equation}
      \label{eq:unit-circle-par-cen}
      \{(u,v) \,\mid\, v = 0\} \to \{ (u',v') \,\mid\,  l_{c_{e}}^2((0,-\frac{\breve{\sigma}}{2}), (u',v'))\cdot(-\breve{\sigma})=1\}, 
    \end{equation}
    where \(l_{c_{e}}^2((0,-\frac{\breve{\sigma}}{2}), (u',v'))= u'^2+\breve{\sigma}
    v'\), see~\eqref{eq:k-center-point}. 

    The image of upper halfplane is:
    \begin{equation}
      \label{eq:unit-disk-par-cen}
                                                               
                                                  
                                                           
                                                   
                                                     
      \{(u,v) \,\mid\, v > 0\} \to 
         \{(u',v') \,\mid\, l_{c_{e}}^2((0, -\frac{\breve{\sigma}}{2}), (u',v'))\cdot(-\breve{\sigma})< 1\}.
    \end{equation}

  \item \label{it:parab-unit-disk-foc} \(P_{\breve{\sigma}}\) with \(\breve{\sigma}\neq0\)
    transforms the ``real axis'' \(U\) to the p-cycle with p-length squared
    \(-\breve{\sigma}\)~\eqref{eq:focal-length} from its h-focus
    \((0,-1-\frac{\breve{\sigma}}{4})\),  and the upper half-plane---to the ``interior'' part of it,
    cf.~\eqref{eq:unit-circle-ell}:
    \begin{eqnarray}
      \label{eq:unit-circle-par-foc}
      \{(u,v) \,\mid\, v = 0\} &\to& \{ (u',v') \,\mid\,
      l_{f_{h}}^2((0,{\textstyle-1-\frac{\breve{\sigma}}{4}}), 
      (u',v'))\cdot( -\breve{\sigma})=1\}, \\
      \label{eq:unit-disk-par-foc}
      \{(u,v) \,\mid\, v > 0\} &\to& \{(u',v') \,\mid\,
      l_{f_{h}}^2((0,{\textstyle-1-\frac{\breve{\sigma}}{4}}), (u',v'))\cdot( -\breve{\sigma})<1\}. 
    \end{eqnarray}
  \item \label{it:parab-unit-disk-p-foc} \(P_{\breve{\sigma}}\)
    transforms the ``real axis'' \(U\) to the cycle with p-length
    \(-\breve{\sigma}\) from its p-focus
    \((0,-1)\),  and the upper half-plane---to the ``interior'' part of it,
    cf.~\eqref{eq:unit-circle-ell}:
    \begin{eqnarray}
      \label{eq:unit-circle-par-p-foc}
      \{(u,v) \,\mid\, v = 0\} &\to& \{ (u',v') \,\mid\,
      l_{f_{p}}^2((0,-1), (u',v')) \cdot( -\breve{\sigma})=1\}, \\
      \label{eq:unit-disk-par-p-foc}
      \{(u,v) \,\mid\, v > 0\} &\to& \{(u',v') \,\mid\,
      l_{f_{p}}^2((0,-1), (u',v'))\cdot( -\breve{\sigma})<1\},
    \end{eqnarray}
    where \(l_{f_{p}}^2((0,-1), (u',v'))=\frac{u'^2}{v'+1}\)~\eqref{eq:focal-length}.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-31 -->
<!-- remark-29: body_md -->
Note that the both elliptic~\eqref{eq:unit-circle-ell} and
  hyperbolic~\eqref{eq:unit-circle-hyp} unit circle descriptions can
  be written uniformly with parabolic
  descriptions~\eqref{eq:unit-circle-par-cen}--\eqref{eq:unit-circle-par-p-foc} as
  \begin{displaymath}
     \{ (u',v') \,\mid\, l^2_{c_{\breve{\sigma}}}(u'e_0+v'e_1)\cdot(-\breve{\sigma})=1\} .
  \end{displaymath}
<!-- end remark-29 -->
<!-- lemma-32: body_md -->
\label{le:n-orbits-concentric}
  \(N\)-orbits in the parabolic cases
  (Fig.~\ref{fig:unit-disks}(\(N_{P_{e}}\), \(N_{P_p}\),
  \(N_{P_{h}}\))) are \emph{concentric parabolas} (or straight lines)
  in the sense of Defn.~\ref{de:center-first} with e-centres at
  \((0,\frac{1}{2})\), \((0,\infty)\), \((0,-\frac{1}{2})\)
  correspondingly.
<!-- end lemma-32 -->
<!-- lemma-33: body_md -->
\label{le:np-orbits-p-confocal}
  The Cayley transform of orbits of the parabolic fix subgroup in
  Fig.~\ref{fig:concentric-equidist}(\(N'_{P_e}\)) are parabolas
  consisting of points on the same
  \(l_{f_p}\)-length~\eqref{eq:k-focus-point} from the point \((0,-1)\),
  cf.~\ref{le:parabolic-disk}.\ref{it:parab-unit-disk-p-foc}.
<!-- end lemma-33 -->
<!-- remark-30: body_md -->
\label{re:par-more-cayley}
  We see that the varieties of possible Cayley transforms in the
  parabolic case is bigger than in the two other cases. It is
  interesting that this parabolic richness is a consequence of the
  parabolic degeneracy of the generator \(e_1^2=0\). Indeed for both
  the elliptic and the hyperbolic signs in \(e_1^2=\pm 1\) only one
  matrix~\eqref{eq:cayley-points} out of two possible \(
  \begin{pmatrix}
    1 & e_1 \\ \pm \sigma e_1 & 1
  \end{pmatrix}\)\vspace{3pt} has a non-zero determinant. And only for
  the degenerate parabolic value \(e_1^2=0\) both these matrices are
  non-singular!
<!-- end remark-30 -->
<!-- lemma-34: body_md -->
Let \({ C^{s}_{a}}\) be a cycle in \(\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}^{\sigma}_{}{}}\).
  \begin{itemize}
  \item[(e, h)] In the elliptic or hyperbolic cases the Cayley
    transform maps a cycle \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) to the composition of its inversion 
    with the reflection
    \({\hat C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}} { C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}{\hat C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) in
    the cycle \({ C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\), where \({\hat C^{s}_{\breve{\sigma}}}=
    \begin{pmatrix}
      \pm \breve{e}_1 && 1\\
      1 && \mp \breve{e}_1
    \end{pmatrix}\)  with \(\breve{\sigma}=\pm1\) (see the first and last drawings on
    Fig.~\ref{fig:unit-disk-all-cases}). 
  \item[(p)] 
    \label{it:cayley-cycle-parab}
    In the parabolic case the Cayley transform maps a cycle
    \((k,l,n,m)\) to the cycle \((k-2\breve{\sigma} n, l, n ,m+2\breve{\sigma} n)\).
  \end{itemize}
<!-- end lemma-34 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \(A\)-orbits in transforms \(P_e\) and \(P_h\) are segments of
    parabolas with the focal length \(\frac{1}{2}\) passing through
    \((0,-\frac{1}{2})\). Their vertices belong to two parabolas
    \(v=\frac{1}{2}(-x^2-1)\) and \(v=\frac{1}{2}(x^2-1)\)
    correspondingly, which are boundaries of parabolic circles in
    \(P_h\) and \(P_e\) (note the swap!).
  \item\label{it:parabolic-disk5}
    \(K\)-orbits in transform \(P_e\)  are parabolas
    with focal length less than \(\frac{1}{2}\) and in transform
    \(P_h\)---with inverse of focal length bigger than \(-2\).
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- lemma-35: body_md -->
An infinitesimal cycle \({ C^{a}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\)~\eqref{eq:inf-cycle} is
  f-orthogonal (in the sense of Lem.~\ref{le:infinitesimal-ortho}.\ref{it:infinitesimal-f-ortho}) to a
  cycle \({\tilde C^{a}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) if and only if the Cayley
  transform~\ref{it:cayley-cycle-parab}(p) of \({ C^{a}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\) is
  f-orthogonal to the Cayley transform of \({\tilde C^{a}_{\breve{\sigma}}}\).
<!-- end lemma-35 -->
